questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish an architecture blueprint from a requirements document?
options: They are exactly the same document under two different names
A requirements document captures what the business needs before a solution is chosen; a blueprint describes the agreed solution after key decisions have been made
A blueprint is always shorter than a requirements document
A requirements document is only used for Salesforce projects involving code
questions.explain: A requirements document captures the need itself, before any solution has been chosen. A blueprint sits later in the process — it records the chosen approach and the decisions behind it, ready for someone else to build or review.

questions.q: Which blueprint section is specifically responsible for stating what's included and what's explicitly excluded?
options: Risks
Scope
Open questions
Context and objective
questions.explain: Scope states what's covered and, just as importantly, what's deliberately excluded, so nobody later assumes something is handled that actually isn't.

questions.q: What should a blueprint's "key decisions and trade-offs" section reuse from an earlier lesson in this chapter?
options: Lesson 7's constraint/assumption distinction
Lesson 9's four-part decision structure: the decision, the drivers, the alternative considered, and the main known risk
Lesson 8's risk-likelihood-and-impact framing exclusively
Nothing; it's an entirely new structure introduced in this lesson
questions.explain: This lesson explicitly shows that the blueprint isn't a new skill — its key-decisions section is built directly from Lesson 9's four-part decision structure (decision, drivers, alternative considered, main known risk).

questions.q: What should a blueprint's "open questions" section contain?
options: Every question that was ever asked during the project, resolved or not
Nothing; a complete blueprint should have zero open questions by definition
Anything genuinely still unresolved, named honestly rather than hidden
Only questions the business sponsor has personally approved listing
questions.explain: A blueprint that pretends everything is settled when it isn't invites a nasty surprise later. Genuinely unresolved questions should be named honestly, and moved into the relevant section once they're actually answered.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe a blueprint as a "living document" rather than a one-time deliverable?
options: Because Salesforce requires blueprints to be resubmitted every quarter
Because an assumption can turn out false, a constraint can change, or a risk can materialize, and the blueprint should be updated to keep describing the solution actually being built
Because blueprints are not allowed to contain diagrams until finalized
Because a living document means it has no fixed sections at all
questions.explain: A blueprint written once and never revisited drifts out of date as real-world surprises occur. Treating it as living means updating it when assumptions, constraints, or risks change, so it keeps reflecting the actual solution rather than the originally imagined one.
